title: Find Median from Data Stream
directAnswer: Maintain two heaps that split the numbers in half: a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half. Keep their sizes balanced (differ by at most one). The median is the top of the larger heap, or the average of both tops when sizes are equal. addNum is O(log n); findMedian is O(1).

remember.pattern: Two balanced heaps (max-heap low half, min-heap high half)
remember.formula:
addNum(x):
    push x onto low (max-heap)
    move low.top -> high      # ensure every low ≤ every high
    if len(high) > len(low):  # rebalance sizes
        move high.top -> low
findMedian():
    if len(low) > len(high): return low.top
    return (low.top + high.top) / 2
rules: `low` is a **max-heap** (its top is the largest of the small half); `high` is a **min-heap** (its top is the smallest of the big half).
Invariant 1 — **order**: every element in `low` ≤ every element in `high`.
Invariant 2 — **balance**: `0 ≤ len(low) − len(high) ≤ 1`. Keep `low` the one that may be larger by one.
Python has only a min-heap — simulate a max-heap by **negating** values pushed to `low`.
The 'push then transfer then rebalance' dance enforces BOTH invariants on every insert without sorting.
whenToUse: Running median / running percentile over a stream of numbers
You need the middle element repeatedly as data arrives
Any 'maintain two halves and query the boundary' design problem
Online algorithm where re-sorting on every query is too slow
antiSignals: Data is static and given upfront → just sort once, O(n log n)
Values are bounded small integers → a counting/Fenwick approach can give O(1) updates
You only need the median once → nth_element / quickselect is O(n)
remember.takeaway: Two heaps facing each other turn 'find the middle of a growing set' into O(log n) inserts and O(1) median reads. Whenever a problem needs the boundary between the smaller and larger halves of streaming data, reach for a max-heap/min-heap pair.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can design a data structure (not just an algorithm) that supports two operations efficiently, and whether you can state and preserve invariants across mutations.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Re-sorting or re-scanning the whole collection on each findMedian (O(n log n) or O(n) per query), or letting the two heaps drift out of balance so the median read is wrong.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the two invariants (order and balance) explicitly, show the push-transfer-rebalance sequence preserves both, and discuss follow-ups: bounded range → counting buckets, and the 99% in [0,100] variant.

problemStatement:
The **median** is the middle value in an ordered list. If the list has an even number of elements, the median is the mean of the two middle values.

Implement the `MedianFinder` class:
- `MedianFinder()` initialises the object.
- `void addNum(int num)` adds the integer `num` from the data stream to the data structure.
- `double findMedian()` returns the median of all elements so far. Answers within 10⁻⁵ of the actual answer are accepted.
constraints: There will be at least one element before findMedian is called
At most 5 × 10⁴ calls to addNum and findMedian
Follow-up: if all numbers are in [0, 100], can you optimise? What if 99% are in [0, 100]?
understanding: Design an object that ingests numbers one at a time and can report the current median on demand. The challenge is that the stream never stops, so we can't sort once — every insert must keep the structure 'median-ready' cheaply.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can findMedian be called before any number is added?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The constraints guarantee at least one addNum first, so I won't handle the empty case — though I'd guard it in production.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How many calls, and what's the read/write mix?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to 5×10⁴ mixed calls. Because findMedian can be called as often as addNum, I want findMedian to be O(1) and addNum O(log n).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the values bounded?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: In general [-10⁵, 10⁵]. The follow-up restricts to [0, 100], which unlocks an O(1)-update counting-array solution.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do duplicates occur?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, duplicates are fine — heaps handle them naturally and the median definition is unaffected.

examples.explanation: After 1,2 the two middles are 1 and 2 → mean 1.5. After adding 3, the ordered set is [1,2,3] → middle is 2.
Single element; it is its own median.
Ordered: [-3,-2,-1]; the middle of three is -2. Negatives behave identically.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Two heaps is the canonical streaming answer; bounded values unlock a counting array.

approaches.name: Sorted Insertion (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: Mention briefly to anchor the cost, then pivot — it's too slow per insert for a real stream.
hints: If you kept the numbers sorted at all times, where would the median always be?
Insert each new number into its correct position in a sorted list (binary search to find the spot).
Finding the spot is O(log n), but shifting elements to insert is O(n) — that's the bottleneck for a long stream.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Binary search locates the insertion point in O(log n), but array insertion shifts up to n elements → O(n) per add. The median is then a direct index lookup, O(1).
approaches.explanation:
Keep an array sorted as numbers arrive. To add, binary-search for the insertion index and splice the value in. The median is then trivially the middle index (odd count) or the average of the two middle indices (even count).

**Why it's tempting.** findMedian becomes a single index calculation — O(1). For a few inserts followed by many median queries, it's even reasonable.

**Why it fails at scale.** The insertion itself shifts elements: adding to the front of a 50,000-element array moves all of them. Across n adds that's O(n²) overall — too slow for the call volume. We need an insert that's logarithmic, which points to heaps.
approaches.insight: Keeping data fully sorted is overkill: the median only needs the *boundary* between the lower and upper halves, not a total order. Tracking just that boundary is what makes the two-heap solution fast.

dryRun.intro: Maintain a sorted list; median is the middle index.

java.explanation: Unsigned shift avoids overflow on (lo+hi) for large indices.
The insertion shifts every later element — the O(n) cost that sinks this approach.
Even count → average the two central elements as a double.

python.explanation: Binary-searches the spot (O(log n)) then inserts, which shifts elements (O(n)).
Odd count → the single middle element is the median.

pitfalls: Assuming list insertion is cheap — it shifts O(n) elements.
Integer division when averaging the two middles — divide by 2.0, not 2.

approaches.name: Two Heaps — Max-Heap Low Half, Min-Heap High Half (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The expected answer. Phrase it as 'split the data into a lower half and an upper half, each kept heap-ordered toward the boundary'.
hints: The median only depends on the boundary between the smaller half and the larger half. What if you stored those two halves separately?
Keep a max-heap of the lower half (so its top is the largest small value) and a min-heap of the upper half (so its top is the smallest large value). The median lives at those two tops.
On each insert, push, then move the boundary element across so every low ≤ every high, then rebalance sizes so they differ by at most one. Median = the larger heap's top, or the average of both tops.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each addNum does a constant number of heap pushes/pops, each O(log n). findMedian just reads one or two heap tops — O(1). Both heaps together hold all n elements → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Picture the sorted stream cut in two. The **lower half** lives in a max-heap `low` (top = the *largest* of the small numbers). The **upper half** lives in a min-heap `high` (top = the *smallest* of the big numbers). The median is precisely at this seam — that's the entire idea.

**Two invariants do all the work.**
- *Order*: every value in `low` ≤ every value in `high`. This guarantees the two tops straddle the true middle.
- *Balance*: the heaps' sizes differ by at most one, and we let `low` be the one allowed to hold the extra element on odd counts.

**The insert dance — push, transfer, rebalance.** Always push the new number onto `low` first. Then pop `low`'s top and push it onto `high`. That transfer guarantees the *order* invariant: whatever the largest of the lower half was, it now sits in the upper half if it belongs there. But the transfer may leave `high` bigger than `low`, breaking *balance* — so if `high` is larger, move its top back to `low`. After this fixed sequence both invariants hold again.

**Reading the median.** If `low` has one more element than `high` (odd total), the median is `low`'s top. If the sizes are equal (even total), the median is the average of the two tops. Both are O(1).

**Python max-heap trick.** `heapq` only offers a min-heap. To make `low` behave as a max-heap, push **negated** values; the smallest negative corresponds to the largest original value. Negate again when you read it back. Forgetting a negation is the #1 bug here.
approaches.insight: The transfer-then-rebalance pattern is a tiny, branch-free way to maintain a sorted partition under insertion. By always routing the newcomer through `low` and shipping the boundary across, you never have to compare the new value against the heap tops yourself — the heaps' own ordering decides where it lands.

dryRun.intro: low = max-heap (lower half), high = min-heap (upper half). Keep |low|−|high| ∈ {0,1}.

steps.action: push 1→low; move 1→high; high bigger → move back to low
push 3→low; move low.top(3)→high; high bigger → move high.top(2)→low

java.explanation: reverseOrder turns Java's default min-heap into a MAX-heap for the lower half.
Step 1: every new value enters low first — uniform routing simplifies the logic.
Step 2: ship low's current max into high, enforcing 'every low ≤ every high'.
Step 3: if high grew larger, move its min back so low is the (possibly) larger heap.
Equal sizes (even total) → median is the average of the two boundary tops.

python.explanation: Negate so heapq's min-heap behaves as a max-heap: smallest negative = largest value.
Pop low's max (un-negate) and push to high — the order-invariant transfer.
Rebalance only when high overtakes low; we keep low ≥ high in size.
Odd total: low holds the extra element, so its (un-negated) top IS the median.

edgeCases.behavior: Push 5→low, move to high, high bigger → move back; low=[5], high=[]. findMedian returns 5.0.
low=[2], high=[2]; median (2+2)/2 = 2.0. Duplicates split across the seam fine.
Each smaller value enters low and the transfer keeps order; balance logic still yields the correct middle.

pitfalls: Forgetting to negate when reading low's top in Python — returns the wrong sign/value.
Comparing the new number to the heap tops manually instead of using push-transfer-rebalance — error-prone branching.
Letting balance drift (rebalancing on the wrong side) so the larger heap isn't consistently `low` — median read picks the wrong top.

commonMistakes: Re-sorting or re-scanning all elements on every findMedian call instead of maintaining heaps incrementally.
In Python, forgetting that heapq is min-only — omitting negation makes `low` a min-heap and breaks the invariant.
Allowing the two heaps to differ in size by more than one, so the boundary tops no longer bracket the median.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forgetting the max-heap negation in Python
commonMistakesDetailed.why: heapq is a min-heap. Without negating, `low` keeps its smallest on top, so `low[0]` is not the largest of the lower half and the median read is wrong.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
heapq.heappush(self.low, num)        # min-heap, wrong end on top
heapq.heappush(self.high, heapq.heappop(self.low))
# findMedian reads self.low[0] expecting the MAX — it's the min
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
heapq.heappush(self.low, -num)       # negate → behaves as max-heap
heapq.heappush(self.high, -heapq.heappop(self.low))
# read -self.low[0] to recover the true max

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Rebalancing on the wrong side
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you let `high` be the heap that may hold the extra element but read the median from `low`, odd counts return the wrong value. Pick one heap (here `low`) to own the surplus and be consistent.

followupVariations.title: Sliding Window Median
followupVariations.hint: Same two heaps, but support removal as the window slides — use lazy deletion or a TreeMap/multiset.

followupVariations.title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
followupVariations.hint: Single size-k heap — a simpler cousin of the boundary-heap idea.

followupVariations.title: Kth Largest Element in a Stream
followupVariations.hint: Maintain a min-heap of size k for the streaming Kth largest — design-problem sibling.

followupVariations.title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
followupVariations.hint: Static median via binary search on the partition — the offline counterpart.

patternNote: Two balanced heaps maintaining a median boundary. The signature design pattern for running median/percentile over a stream. For bounded values switch to a counting array; for windows add removal support (Sliding Window Median).
